title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony
description: Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.A string of black and white photos shared
body: Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.A string of black and white photos shared by the Flowers singer on Instagram showed the pair kissing while surrounded by white roses.Her mother, Trisha Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, could be seen in the background of one image. Her father Billy Ray Cyrus was not in the picture but was at the ceremony with his partner, actress Liz Hurley.Grammy-winning Cyrus, 33, wore a white silk dress designed by Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent, while 28-year-old drummer Morando said "I do" in a black suit from the same fashion house.In one of the photographs, which was the first in a series of images shared by the singer in an Instagram post, the newly weds posed next to a golden retriever.The post was captioned with "M+M" followed by a white heart and the ceremony date, 21 November.Miley's sister Brandi Cyrus, singer Doechii and fashion designer Donatella Versace were among those to congratulate the couple in the comments.The ceremony reportedly took place at a resort formerly owned by Fly Me To The Moon singer Frank Sinatra.Guests stuck to an all-black dress code, according to reports.The American singer confirmed her engagement to the 28-year-old drummer during an interview with US TV show Good Morning America last year.She said Morando had got down on one knee for the proposal during a trip to Asia."I am not easy to surprise because I love to control every situation and I had completely surrendered and I'm telling you, I was so, so, so surprised," she said.During an interview with Wonderland, Morando said he "had to be really sneaky" to keep his proposal plans a secret."We went to Tokyo first for a couple days, and then on to Kyoto. I think she had a sense that it was coming, so I was waiting until the very last moment of the very last day to throw her off the scent as much as I could," he said.Cyrus, 33, had previously been married to Australian actor Liam Hemsworth but the couple separated in 2019.The singer, whose hits include Party in the U.S.A and Wrecking Ball, married Hunger Games star Hemsworth in 2018 after the couple were in a relationship for a decade.Speaking to British Vogue in 2023, Cyrus said she and 28-year-old Morando met after being "put on a blind date".Morando is a drummer with LA-based band Liily. The band participated in NBC's Miley's New Year's Eve Party - hosted by Cyrus - in 2022, alongside musicians including Cyrus's late godmother Dolly Parton and David Byrne.

schema.headline: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony

title: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis
description: An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.L
body: An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.Named after the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery."The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier.""I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off."I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external. A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics"."We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

schema.headline: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis

title: COP31 climate talks fail to reach deal amid fossil fuel and money rows
description: Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talk
body: Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures. The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times"."That is the reality," he said on Monday.After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday to try to break the deadlock.But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change". "It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions. Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts. Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room."Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing"."This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change. The UN says the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century. Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says. But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.The COP31 president also said more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035.But following the weekend's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world. The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia."[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" on Sunday.The UN climate process has "suffered setbacks before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

schema.headline: COP31 climate talks fail to reach deal amid fossil fuel and money rows

title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
description: Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged marke
body: Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO)  price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth."As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said."Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.But tech stocks more broadly also fell.Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

schema.headline: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide

title: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
description: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "frien
body: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said. Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war"."They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer"."I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure". The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said.  Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare"."This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

schema.headline: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend

title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
description: Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when
body: Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight."She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue."He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen"."She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".After telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" said an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.During the conversation, Khristina said she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did."That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent."Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina."And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025. He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.As Khristina and the FBI heard all of this, law enforcement were staging to bring Jenny to safety, after being alerted to her whereabouts.While Harmel was out of the home, officers were sent to the street and the address, and Khristina was prepping Jenny for her run to freedom.She'd unsuccessfully tried escaping before, she told Khristina.Law enforcement was "phenomenal…giving me an update, you know, 'We're nine minutes out, we're seven minutes out,'" says Khristina, who was on the phone with Jenny the entire time, her son Landon watching at her side.Khristina could hear other people in the home with Jenny, and she was afraid that someone would catch wind of what was happening and harm the girl.But she kept any of those fears from Jenny."I want you to take three deep breaths with me," she told the teen. "When an officer tells me to go, and I relay that message to you, I want you to run up those stairs as fast as you can … Grab that basement door."I want you to keep going down that hallway and grab that front door… do not stop.'"The mother and son watched breathlessly as Jenny ran into the arms of a state trooper.Harmel is now in federal custody and has been charged in a criminal complaint with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Local Oregon media also reported he'd been accused of sexually abusing a six-year-old in the months before Jenny disappeared - and a sexual abuse protective order was granted against him in March 2025.He remains behind bars awaiting trial.A lawyer for the defendant did not respond to a BBC request for comment.Jenny, meanwhile, remains in daily communication with Khristina and Landon - who still enjoys playing online games with her."Sometimes we just sit on video chat, just so she knows she has someone that cares," Khristina says. "She was on video last night when I cooked dinner …it's nice to know that when she has a bad day or a bad moment, she can call me right away or call Landon right away.""She's doing great for what she's gone through."They haven't met in person yet, but they're in the process of trying to make that happen."I hope I can put my arms around her soon," Khristina says.

schema.headline: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl

title: 'El Chapo Isidro': Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
description: A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isi
body: A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said. Seven suspects were killed in the operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, the secretariat added.Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.Meza Flores, his cousin, and his brother-in-law were flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said. The other five remained in the state of Sinaloa.Authorities also said they had seized multiple weapons during the operation, including a grenade launcher, as well as drugs and cash.The US Consulate General in the city of Hermosillo said it was "monitoring reports of ongoing security operations, armed clashes, road blockades, and vehicle fires that occurred overnight in Ahome, Guamúchil, Guasave, and Navolato" following the arrest of Meza-Flores.  It advised US citizens to remain alert for potential violence in the area and for residents to remain sheltered in place.When Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.

schema.headline: 'El Chapo Isidro': Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out

title: Michel Zecler: Police officers sentenced for beating of music producer
description: Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated
body: Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.All were told they could never serve in the police again.The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.The case was heard by a panel of five judges.The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

schema.headline: Michel Zecler: Police officers sentenced for beating of music producer

title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
description: Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "init
body: Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.Russia's embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.In a statement, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia". Russian state media cite the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly". In a statement on Saturday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "I strongly condemn the assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services."This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable," she said, adding that "Russia's hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real."The rapper's real name is Albert Vasiliev.PET said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September. Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said. He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Copenhagen was already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians could still get a Schengen visa in another country and travel to Denmark. Copenhagen wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

schema.headline: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper

title: South Africa's local elections: ANC fights to keep control of cities after election setback
description: While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.Bu
body: While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.It emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.This is what voters want.The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.Experts agree that even after new arrangements take effect, it will take longer than a five-year term to resolve the issues facing many municipalities, particularly South Africa's biggest city Johannesburg."I think if we are really turning the ship around, we are talking about a 10-year period," Duvenhage said.Swana echoed this, saying it would take a decade to "cleanse and purify" local councils and "reinstate them as "proper municipalities".

schema.headline: South Africa's local elections: ANC fights to keep control of cities after election setback

title: Philippines pet dumping: Dead dogs and cats were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
description: The livestream begins.A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of p
body: The livestream begins.A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.Names are written on the packages – Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet – and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs.""Purebreds," says the woman filming.Warning: This story contains images some might find upsettingIn the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.Chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.On 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.Chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting – taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page."I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know."In the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged."The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message."When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.By crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals.  "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris says. "Others were liquefied."LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.Their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.Some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?As more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila."So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," says Chris. "And man, it just flooded in."The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths."Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a big thing with the boom of the pet industry," says Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets."These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.Or not, as the case may be.Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, says she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.Calling says Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated."Pet owners entrust these services with something very important: the remains of a beloved family member," she says. "We need to know what happened."Earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.According to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT – but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law – estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them – and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.Two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The company is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.The BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm said the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, says she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago."I just can't accept the pain of not knowing what might have happened to him," she says. "I really want to confirm whether Harvey was properly cremated, and whether the ashes I received were truly his."Many are wrestling with the same uncertainty. As Cabrera puts it: "God knows what that was inside those urns."In response to those anxieties, a veterinarian in nearby Quezon City has started offering complimentary forensic ash testing. For those whose pets have been found among the bodies, other crematoriums have offered to do the job properly, and for free.The animal welfare society, Paws, is volunteering legal services to help people file complaints with the authorities, and has received more than 150 requests so far. It is also calling for a nationwide audit of all pet cremation businesses.On 2 November, Percival Vilar Cendaña of the Philippines' progressive Akbayan Party appeared on national television. He was there to speak about the pet-dumping scandal, which, in the span of a few days, had flared into a national disgrace."Our worst fears have been confirmed," he told the Bilyonaryo news channel. "Now we see that these are not isolated incidents. It is true that this is a syndicate that is conducting widespread operations."Neither the police nor the NBI have confirmed that the dumpings were carried out by a "syndicate", nor that they were "widespread". Many details surrounding the case remain murky. But the hysteria is real – and Cendaña was giving voice to a common sentiment."Those who deceived these poor fur parents should be jailed," he said.At least three individuals have surrendered to the NBI and been charged with violating the city's Code of Sanitation, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, and the Sanitation Code of the Philippines.But many feel this doesn't go far enough, and say it fails to hold anyone liable for the way the animals' remains were treated.Cabrera says the country's animal-cruelty law doesn't cover the treatment of animals after death. And "there's no crime if there's no law".The scandal has prompted a groundswell to change that. Lawmakers like Cendaña are pushing for a national commission on animal welfare to ensure their dignity in life and death.Meanwhile, Cabrera says Paws will seek "moral and exemplary" damages on behalf of aggrieved pet owners.One woman whose dog was suspected to have been found among the dumped bodies told the BBC she couldn't speak about it because she was "feeling weak"."I haven't slept for three days from all the crying," she said.Chris has also been losing sleep, taking calls from grieving pet owners who have watched his videos. "Hundreds of people call me in tears, just sobbing," he says. "They're in so much pain. And half the time you're telling them: 'you're not going to find your pet. It's been too long; we're not going to be able to identify it.' And it just crushes them."As well as new laws, Chris wants stricter enforcement of existing rules. He wants to know how he managed to unearth so much in the space of a fortnight, and why people keep coming to him saying they don't trust the police to take their concerns seriously, he says.The BBC contacted Philippine National Police (PNP) for comment, but didn't hear back. Earlier this month, PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr said authorities were determined to hold accountable those who allegedly took advantage of grieving pet owners, saying such exploitation "must be addressed with the full force of the law", according to ABS-CBN."Fraud is not measured solely by the amount of money taken, but also by the damage inflicted on the people whose trust has been betrayed," Nartatez said."To the affected pet owners, we recognise the pain and distress this incident has caused your families."Yet the police themselves have come under official scrutiny.On Monday, the National Police Commission announced an investigation into officers in Cavite and Bulacan after they suggested LAFS might be involved in the pet dumping because they were often first on the scene. The officers did not present evidence for their claims. The investigation also covers reports that officers visited the Taylors' home and took photographs.Meanwhile, countless grieving pet owners are suspended in purgatory: desperate for closure on what happened to their dogs and cats, and calling on authorities to do more."We want the case to be properly investigated and those responsible to be held accountable," says Calling.  "I believe that no secret remains hidden forever."Legada, for her part, says: "I just want to find out what really happened to Harvey and where his remains are. I want to know whether he was properly cremated."She also wants people to know: "You can't trust anyone these days."With additional reporting by Virma Simonette Rivera

schema.headline: Philippines pet dumping: Dead dogs and cats were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream

title: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
description: The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filin
body: The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows."To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days."There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant  will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states. It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place. Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible. Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen."There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement. The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a new motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing. The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.

schema.headline: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order

title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
description: The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Repr
body: The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called. Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats. View the 2026 midterm election resultsSunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%."I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable. Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."Foxx, meanwhile, said in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa. Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters. Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website. The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes. Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law. However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

schema.headline: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat

title: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
description: A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer after 14 hours, in overnight Russian strikes on Dymer, in the
body: A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer after 14 hours, in overnight Russian strikes on Dymer, in the Kyiv region, that killed ten people, Ukrainian officials have said.The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said. A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday. Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life. Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.Response teams including police, explosive technicians, dog handlers and medics are continuing with rescue efforts. In a telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.

schema.headline: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say

title: Mamdani reveals plan for closure of New York's Rikers Island jail
description: New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of
body: New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.  Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population. Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates. Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.  It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said. The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein. It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union. "[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges." Kaplan disagreed."It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said. The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays. Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility. In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it. New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan. Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029,  two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032. The mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours. Mamdani said his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across New York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process. He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health issues. Kaplan said Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.  The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.

schema.headline: Mamdani reveals plan for closure of New York's Rikers Island jail
